meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People don't care how much you know until they know how much you care'?
meta.ogDescription: No — Theodore Roosevelt never said it. It’s an anonymous modern adage first documented around 1959, decades after his death.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — an anonymous modern adage
answer.authorDates: 1858–1919 · 26th U.S. President — but not the source of this line
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Theodore Roosevelt ever said or wrote this. Both Quote Investigator ↗ and the Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ classify it as unverified. QI traces it to an anonymous 20th-century adage — the earliest documented version is a 1959 nursing-school commencement address, four decades after TR’s death.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: People don’t care how much you know until they know how much you care.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no evidence that Theodore Roosevelt used this expression” and traces the saying to an anonymous modern origin.

The earliest match QI located is a 1959 commencement address by Margaret Tyson, Dean of the School of Nursing at the University of Virginia, in a variant form; by 1962 the Beltone Hearing Aid Company ↗ manual carried a close version.
Zig Ziglar popularized the phrasing in his 1978 book See You at the Top, which helped cement it as a business-motivation staple — still without any Roosevelt source.
The Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ lists it as a quote for which “no known source can be found to verify the attribution.”
source.excerptNote: The wording itself is unstable across early sightings — a hallmark of a folk adage rather than a quotation from a fixed text. The 1959 version reads “People won’t care how much you know unless they really know how much you care”; the 1962 Beltone manual reads “People don’t care how much you know—until they know how much you care.”
source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous modern adage with no single identifiable author or first-publication source; the earliest documented sightings date to 1959–1962 in variant forms. Because no fixed original work can be tied to the line, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: About the misattribution magnet
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt (1858–1919) was the 26th U.S. President, a prolific author, and one of the most quoted figures in American life — which makes him a favorite magnet for feel-good sayings he never uttered. His genuine writings and speeches are extensively documented, and this warm bit of people-skills wisdom is nowhere among them.

cite.sourceCitation: Garson O’Toole (Quote Investigator), “Quote Origin: People Don’t Care How Much You Know Until They Know How Much You Care,” July 4, 2024. Earliest documented use: Margaret Tyson commencement address, 1959; Beltone Hearing Aid Company manual, 1962.

copyAttribution: Anonymous modern adage — often misattributed to Theodore Roosevelt, but with no evidence he said it. Earliest documented use dates to 1959 (Margaret Tyson) and 1962 (Beltone). Via Quote Investigator.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Roosevelt” quotes on the internet, plastered across LinkedIn, coaching decks, and inspirational posters. The trouble is that no one has ever tied it to a single word Theodore Roosevelt actually spoke or wrote.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no evidence that Theodore Roosevelt used this expression,” and the Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ marks it unverified. TR died in 1919, decades before the saying is first documented.

items.scope: Other names it gets pinned on
items.why: The line is also credited to motivational figures such as Zig Ziglar (who used it in his 1978 See You at the Top) and John C. Maxwell. Per QI ↗, these are later popularizers of an already-circulating adage, not its source.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: it’s an anonymous modern adage. The earliest documented version is a 1959 nursing-school commencement address, per Quote Investigator ↗ — no Roosevelt required.

context.heading: Why the misattribution sticks
lead: The saying captures a genuine truth about leadership and teaching — that trust precedes influence — so it feels like something a plain-spoken, big-hearted leader would say. Theodore Roosevelt, endlessly quotable and long dead, is the path of least resistance for any warm aphorism in search of a pedigree.

Its wording drifts from sighting to sighting (“People won’t care… unless they really know,” “People don’t care… until they know”), which is exactly how folk adages behave and exactly how fixed quotations do not.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator notes the phrasing was popularized in mid-20th-century sales and self-improvement circles — Beltone’s 1962 training manual and Zig Ziglar’s 1978 bestseller both carried it — long before it acquired a presidential signature online.
context.pull: A true saying in search of a famous author — and Roosevelt was the nearest one lying around.
